newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian opposition win prompts govt policy review.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian opposition win prompts govt policy review.

text.p: Bulgaria's ex-communist government, decisively rejected by angry voters in Sunday's presidential election, pledged to launch a thorough policy overhaul early next year.
"We have important, radical and maybe painful decisions to take in the interests of the country," Socialist Prime Minister Zhan Videnov told reporters.
He said a party congress could be held as early as January 1997 and did not rule out cabinet changes.
Videnov called the victory of the opposition UDF in the run-off for the presidency "an impressive win" and congratulated its candidate, 44-year-old lawyer Petar Stoyanov.
First official results, with around one quarter of polling stations counted, showed Stoyanov had won 61.9 percent of the vote against 38.1 percent for the Socialist candidate Ivan Marazov.
Full results are due by Wednesday.
As his supporters took to the streets waving blue UDF flags, Stoyanov pledged to bring his country closer to the European Union and NATO.

But he was careful to avoid direct criticism of the Socialists and proposed a National Salvation Council of experts and respected public figures to advise the government on how to fight the country's deep economic crisis.
"Political independence and economic stability come through integration into the European Union and the Atlantic Alliance," Stoyanov told a news conference.
Bulgaria has the lowest level of foreign investment of the east European former Soviet satellites, and a lingering tendency to seek guidance from Moscow rather than Brussels.
Sunday's vote took place against a background of falling living standards and fears of food and power shortages in the coming Balkan winter.
Even workers in the smokestack industries of the red heartland said they had deserted the Socialists, who won a majority in parliamentary elections in December 1994.
Bombings and other violence have marred Bulgaria's second presidential campaign since the fall of communism in 1989, culminating in the murder last month of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov.
Shortly after voting began, a caller telephoned a bomb threat to a city centre school where President Zhelyu Zhelev was due to cast his ballot. A thorough search found nothing, state radio said.
Zhelev, a pro-market liberal like Stoyanov, lost a U.S.-style primary in June and has not stood for re-election.
The vote coincided with an International Monetary Fund mission discussing terms for release of a delayed $115 million credit vital to stop Bulgaria defaulting on its foreign debt.
Mission leader Anne McGuirk, who arrived on Friday, met Videnov on Sunday but made no comment.
Stoyanov accuses the government of moving too slowly to privatise state firms and close big loss-makers.
Bulgaria has managed to privatise a mere five percent of state industry, with most of the cash going into the pockets of shadowy business groupings close to the Socialists.
